title: From Samba to the Oscars: The Power of Brazilian Culture Worldwide
subtitle: Music that changed global pop, telenovelas seen in over a hundred countries, best-sellers translated into dozens of languages and a cuisine that became a worldwide craze: Brazil is a cultural powerhouse — yet often doesn’t realize it.
excerpt: From bossa nova to açai, from Globo’s telenovelas to Paulo Coelho: a map of Brazil’s global cultural influence and what it means for jobs and soft power.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
Few countries export as much culture as Brazil — and still, the average Brazilian tends to underestimate the reach of what the nation produces. From bossa nova that became a universal soundtrack to the Oscar won by national cinema, from telenovelas watched in more than a hundred countries to açai sold on street corners in California and Tokyo, Brazilian culture is a consolidated global powerhouse. Understanding this force — and what it means for jobs, tourism and influence — is to understand one of the country’s biggest strategic assets.

Music: From Tropical Exoticism to a Global Chart-Topper

The gateway for Brazilian culture to the world was music — and its first great ambassador was Carmen Miranda. In the 1940s, the Rio-born singer became one of Hollywood’s highest-paid stars, bringing samba, albeit stylized and fruit-clad, to screens worldwide. Two decades later, bossa nova did something deeper: it reshaped the language of global popular music. “The Girl from Ipanema,” by Tom Jobim and Vinicius de Moraes, became one of the most covered songs in history, and the “Getz/Gilberto” album — a collaboration between João Gilberto and American saxophonist Stan Getz — won the Grammy for Album of the Year, a historic accolade for Brazilian music at the heart of the American industry.

Later came the Tropicalia of Caetano Veloso and Gilberto Gil, praised by musicians and critics worldwide; the enduring international success of Sérgio Mendes; and, in the heavy-music arena, Sepultura, which rose from Belo Horizonte to become a global metal reference. More recently, streaming shortened the distance: Rio’s funk took over foreign dance floors and producers, and Anitta carried a Spanish-language track to the top of Spotify’s global chart — proof that Brazilian music no longer needs English to travel.

Telenovela: An Industry of Stories with a Brazilian Accent

If music paved the way, the telenovela built an industry. Since the 1970s, Brazil developed its own model of television drama — daily episodes, sophisticated production, social themes woven into the soap opera — which became a wildly successful export. Brazilian telenovelas have been sold to more than a hundred countries and dubbed into dozens of languages. “Escrava Isaura” became a ratings phenomenon in places as diverse as China, Cuba and Poland; decades later, “Avenida Brasil” repeated the feat, proving that Rio’s suburbs could move audiences on the other side of the globe.

This narrative accumulation is today one of the reasons global streaming platforms invest in production in Brazil: few places gather as many screenwriters, actors and technicians trained in the art of crafting long-form stories for massive audiences.

Literature: From Machado to Coelho, Two Extremes That Captivated Readers

In literature, Brazil exports through two very different channels. On one hand, Paulo Coelho turned “The Alchemist” into one of the best-selling and most-translated books of all time, with editions in dozens of languages — an editorial phenomenon few living authors match. On the other, Brazilian high literature is undergoing an international revival: new translations have elevated Clarice Lispector to cult-author status among English-speaking readers and writers, and Machado de Assis, the nation’s greatest classic, is being praised by foreign critics as one of the great novelists of the 19th century, compared unabashedly to European and American masters. Before them, Jorge Amado had already taken his mythic Bahia to readers in dozens of countries.

Gastronomy: From Everyday Coffee to Amazonian Haute Cuisine

At the table, Brazil’s presence starts with the country’s most famous commodity: for more than a century Brazil has been the world’s largest producer and exporter of coffee — much of what the planet drinks each morning is grown on Brazilian soil. But national cuisine has gone far beyond the bean. The rodízio steak-house model turned into an international business, with Brazilian chains operating from the United States to Asia. Açai leapt from Rio’s beaches to become a global health-food craze. The caipirinha entered the classic repertoire of bars worldwide, and pão de queijo and brigadeiro have received gourmet versions in foreign capitals.

At the top of the pyramid, Brazilian chefs have put the country on the haute-cuisine map: São Paulo restaurants have long ranked among the world’s most awarded, featuring menus that showcase Amazonian ingredients such as tucupi, jambu and even saúva ants — turning Brazil’s biodiversity into avant-garde culinary language.

Film: The Long-Awaited Recognition

Brazilian cinema has always earned festival prestige — “Central do Brasil” and “City of God” marked generations and received Oscar nominations — but the ultimate accolade arrived with Walter Salles’s “I’m Still Here,” which gave Brazil its first International Feature Film Oscar, while Fernanda Torres won the Golden Globe for Best Actress in a Drama — echoing, on a larger scale, the stir that her mother, Fernanda Montenegro, had caused in the country decades earlier. The achievement was not a flash in the pan: it crowned decades of accumulated talent, film schools and audiovisual support policies.

Why This Matters for Your Wallet

Soft power — a country’s ability to influence through charm rather than force — often sounds abstract. It isn’t. Culture is economics: the creative sector employs millions of Brazilians, from musicians and technicians to screenwriters, chefs, designers and producers. Every exported telenovela, every international tour, every awarded restaurant generates foreign exchange, attracts tourists and opens doors for other national products. Countries that have strategically invested in cultural export, such as South Korea with K-pop and its series, have shown that the return multiplies — in image, trade and tourism.

For the average reader, the lesson is two-fold. First: valuing domestic production isn’t a patriotic gimmick; it’s an investment — a ticket to Brazilian cinema, a record from a local artist and a book by a national author fund the next generation that will represent the country abroad. Second: real professional opportunities exist in this market, from audiovisual production to gastronomy, from design to cultural tourism — careers that are growing precisely because the world wants to consume Brazil.

A Country That Exports Itself Better Than It Sees Itself

Capoeira circles academies from Berlin to Tokyo and has been recognized by UNESCO as an intangible cultural heritage of humanity. Rio’s carnival ranks among the planet’s biggest celebrations. The list of symbols is almost endless — and they all point to the same conclusion: Brazilian culture has already won over the world; Brazil still needs to treat this achievement as the strategic asset it is, with state policy, continuous investment and informed pride. Until that happens fully, the world keeps dancing, watching, reading and eating Brazil — often without Brazilians themselves realizing the magnitude of what they helped create.
